A race that should’ve barely garnered any attention outside its home state is turning into one of the hottest of the midterms, as Republican Senator Roger Marshall is in the fight of his life against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Six months ago, Democratic hopes for the Senate were centered on Maine, Ohio, and Michigan, maybe even Florida at the outer edges. Nobody was talking about Kansas. Now Emerson has Hamilton ahead 45–43, the New York Times/Siena poll has the race tied at 45, and YouGov has Hamilton leading 48–45. These are consistent, margin-of-error leads for a Democrat.
Marshall is a throwback religious conservative from the pre-Trump era who’s plugged himself into the MAGA universe through faith-and-family politics. He has the votes you’d expect, including a controversial one involving January 6. Hamilton is a centrist Democrat who founded his own church in 1990 with four people in a borrowed space. He’s using that religious background and his charisma as a leader of men to say, “I’m not asking you to vote for a Democrat. I’m asking you to vote for common sense.”
Hamilton wants congressional approval for tariffs, more agricultural export promotion, and year-round guest-worker visas. Those positions push directly against Trump’s tariffs and hard-line immigration policies. Marshall, meanwhile, has to defend Trump during what’s being called “Farmageddon.” Diesel prices can only stay this high for so long. Restrictions on selling crops can only remain this punitive before farmers go crazy.
Marshall’s medical career has also become a liability. An investigation found that he sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical debt, and court records showed 81 arrests after people missed court appearances connected to those cases. His side says the collections were necessary to sustain medical care and that nobody was criminally convicted simply for being unable to pay. But Hamilton has an effective ad featuring a woman who says she was arrested while eight months pregnant after missing a payment. “I’m a doctor” is usually a good political pitch. Marshall found a way to make it a negative.
This isn’t simply the national environment. Republicans face similar problems with farmers, diesel, and tariffs in Iowa, but Ashley Hinson is still leading her Democratic opponent and running ahead of the Republican gubernatorial candidate. Kansas is the combination of a bad environment and an incumbent who’s never been tested suddenly finding himself in the race of his life. The cavalry is arriving: Marshall has hired Chris Grant of Big Dog Strategies, and the Senate Leadership Fund is bringing in nearly $8.2 million, possibly redirected from Georgia and North Carolina. My gut says Kansas is much closer than it should be but doesn’t tip. Raw political gravity and the Republican registration advantage probably carry Marshall through. Maybe.
The broader Republican strategy is now triage. Two Republican super PACs are withdrawing support from Tom Kean Jr. and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, leaving both incumbents without the air cover they expected. Republicans aren’t trying to flip Democratic seats anymore; they’re defending their own and attempting to minimize the losses. Trump is even heading to Wasilla to campaign for Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan against Mary Peltola. Second-term presidents aren’t usually eager to do a full-court press, let alone fly to Alaska. Trump deserves credit for doing the work, but the fact that he’s campaigning in red states tells you where Republican priorities are. They’re no longer on offense.

The Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case over whether Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency has to turn over records about its operations under public records law.
Getting into it: The justices on Tuesday took up a Trump administration appeal in a lawsuit brought by watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), which has been seeking DOGE records since early 2025. It all comes down to how DOGE should be classified.
CREW argues DOGE was a federal agency wielding independent power and is therefore subject to the Freedom of Information Act, while the administration says it was a presidential advisory body, which typically keeps its records out of reach of FOIA requests. US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in March 2025 that DOGE was “likely” covered by FOIA and ordered it to hand over documents, and an appeals court panel agreed. The case has already reached the Supreme Court once.
In June 2025, the conservative majority ruled that Cooper’s order was too broad and blocked a deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason, over the dissent of the three liberal justices. CREW has since narrowed its request, saying it now seeks only DOGE guidance to staff on canceling contracts and firing federal workers, not White House communications. The administration appealed again after losing a second time in the lower courts. Arguments are expected early next year, with a ruling by the end of June.
CREW lawyer Nikhel Sus said DOGE has lost at every level below the Supreme Court, adding that the American people “deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government.” The group says undisputed facts, including Trump’s own statements, show DOGE “was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government.”
This all comes as DOGE’s operations have largely wound down after Musk’s departure last year, and after a Government Accountability Office report found errors in some of DOGE’s savings claims, including figures with no backing and cuts that started before DOGE did.

sources.text:
Supreme Court agrees to take on Trump's appeal over access to DOGE records
Washington DC - The Supreme Court announced on Tuesday it will review an appeal by the administration of Donald Trump to restrict access to records of the Department of Government Efficiency.
The now-defunct agency was launched in 2025 and headed by tech billionaire Elon Musk with the task of cutting government spending, leading to the dismissal of thousands of federal employees and slashing millions in foreign aid.
DOGE was highly active during the first 100 days of Trump's second term, but significantly pulled back after Musk had a public falling out with the president in May 2025, and was completely shut down by July 4 this year.
An NGO called Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed the initial lawsuit, requesting government records from DOGE under the Freedom of Information Act, which requires federal agencies to provide documents to any member of the public who requests them.
The Trump administration maintains DOGE was not a formal government agency and was thus not required to respond to FOIA requests.
The Supreme Court had previously paused a lower court decision that ruled in favor of CREW, sending the case back to lower courts for more litigation on which records DOGE was required to hand over. The six conservative justices on the bench sided against the three liberal ones.
Now the issue returns to the Supreme Court's docket this term, which ends in late June.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Grants Trump Admin Request in Pivotal DOGE Case
sources.text:
Supreme Court Grants Trump Admin Request in Pivotal DOGE Case
The Supreme Court granted a Trump administration request Tuesday to examine lower court rulings regarding record requests related to the Department of Government Efficiency.
A watchdog group, Citizens for Responsibilities and Ethics, is seeking information about how much power DOGE had over federal spending cuts and its general authority over federal agencies, Politico reported.
Trump officials are arguing that DOGE acted in an advisory capacity and did not make the final call on spending cuts, firings, or any other major changes.
If the high court rejects that premise, DOGE could be forced to hand over its records under the Freedom of Information Act.
Solicitor General John Sauer filed an emergency appeal to the justices last year, asking them to block the discovery that lower courts approved.
In an unsigned order, the Supreme Court said that the lower-court rulings were “not appropriately tailored” and that courts must show “deference and restraint” when dealing with the executive branch.
The three liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
The watchdog group then scaled back its records request, and the process was allowed to move forward. Sauer went back to the high court in March, arguing that the lower courts had sidestepped their previous ruling.
“The lower courts’ approach also defeats FOIA’s objective of protecting the separation of powers,” Justice Department lawyers wrote. “Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA’s reach.”
CREW’s chief counsel Nikhel Sus, on the other hand, said lower courts have consistently ruled that the organization has a right to examine DOGE’s records to find out how much authority it was granted.
“The lower courts have uniformly ruled that CREW is entitled to discovery in this case to help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to FOIA,” he declared.
“We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government,” Sus concluded.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk led DOGE when it was first formed at the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, serving as a Special Government Employee and Senior Advisor to the commander in chief.
Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told Newsweek, however, that DOGE was more of a “one-off” and has since “fizzled out.”
“I don’t think it’ll have broad implications in terms of discovery requests to federal agencies because those agencies are authorized by Congress,” he explained. “They receive funds. The heads of those agencies — they make decisions, so I really think this is more of a one-off.”
The case will likely be argued before the Supreme Court some time next year.

US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records
The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from freedom of information requirements.
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear arguments in a watchdog’s lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
The high court is intervening on Tuesday for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (CREW) in Washington’s case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of US President Donald Trump’s second term. The Trump administration asked the court to hear the case.
Last year, the high court reined in a district court’s order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court’s conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group.
CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).
The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA’s requirements as a presidential advisory body.
Cooper ruled in CREW’s favour and ordered expedited processing of the group’s records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW.
The Trump administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court’s direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the “autonomy and confidentiality” of presidential advisers.
“Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA’s reach,” US Department of Justice lawyers wrote.
The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorised the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason.
CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court’s previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025.
“Undisputed facts in the public record — including the President’s statements — confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government,” CREW lawyers wrote.
In a statement Tuesday, CREW lawyer Nikhel Sus said the lower courts have uniformly ruled that it is entitled to records that could help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to the Freedom of Information Act.
“We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government,” Sus said in the statement.
DOGE said it had slashed tens of billions of dollars in expenditures, but its claims were difficult for outside financial experts to verify.
Federal auditors found that some of DOGE’s reported savings across contract, grant and lease terminations were incorrect, lacked supporting evidence or included terminations that were already under way when DOGE was established, according to a report by the Government Accountability Office.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to decide whether Trump can shield DOGE documents from public view
Supreme Court to review access to U.S. DOGE Service records
Supreme Court makes its move in Trump’s fight to keep DOGE’s secrets buried
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk during the "A New Golden Age" summit at the U.S. Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, DC, US, October 8, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci REFILE - CORRECTING FROM "NATIONAL MEDAL OF TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION" TO "NATIONAL MEDAL OF SCIENCE".
The Supreme Court granted a Justice Department request to review an order that could expose how much power the White House’s cost-cutting office wielded over firings and spending cuts across the government.
The justices granted the petition Tuesday, according to the court’s docket. The government is fighting a lawsuit by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington seeking records from the Department of Government Efficiency, officially known as the U.S. DOGE Service.
CREW argues the office wielded enough independent power to fall under the Freedom of Information Act. It’s the second time the case has reached the justices, who last year reined in an earlier order, the Associated Press reported.
The order under review lets CREW seek evidence, a process known as discovery, about the office’s directives to cancel contracts and fire workers. It also lets CREW seek information about the office’s access to sensitive data, records on its employees, and sworn testimony from its leader, according to the Justice Department’s brief.
“Perhaps most dramatically, the court of appeals summarily approved the deposition of a high-level presidential advisor—USDS Administrator Amy Gleason—without even acknowledging that it was doing so,” the brief said.
“[D]iscovery into sensitive interbranch communications risks chilling future communications by presidential advisors who will have to fear having their advice disclosed in litigation,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.
“USDS has already made clear that it has issued no binding directives to agencies because it lacks the legal authority to do so,” Sauer argued.
In February 2025, CNN’s Alayna Treene asked White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt whether the office’s staff had real authority, including power to make hiring and firing decisions, Treene wrote on X.
“DOGE does not have statutory authority. DOGE is advising...It’s ultimately up to the discretion of these secretaries to make these hirings & firings,” Leavitt said.
Statutory authority is power Congress grants. The government’s brief makes the same case, calling the office “a purely advisory body.” If sworn evidence shows that advice functioned as orders, the White House’s own description of the office could turn into a liability.
Courts in other cases have already used evidence of the office’s role to void its actions, including in May, when U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon in New York ordered the National Endowment for the Humanities to restore more than 1,400 grants worth more than $100 million.
Documents revealed in discovery in that case showed DOGE staffers used ChatGPT to flag grants for cancellation, according to Inside Higher Ed.
“DOGE had no statutory authority to terminate NEH grants,” McMahon wrote, according to Minnesota Lawyer. “And on the undisputed evidence, DOGE — not the NEH Chairperson or anyone else at NEH — effectuated the terminations at issue here.”
In March, in a separate case brought by nonprofit groups, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan allowed claims to proceed that DOGE’s leader needed Senate confirmation before allegedly directing federal workforce actions.
CREW’s June brief opposing review described “massive changes across the federal government,” including former White House adviser Elon Musk’s announcement of canceled contracts “worth billions of dollars.” The brief also cited the office’s “unprecedented access to sensitive personal and classified data and payment systems.”
“This appeal is an obvious delay tactic to keep the American public in the dark about DOGE’s reckless operation and disastrous impact,” CREW President Donald K. Sherman said after the petition was filed in March.
CREW chief counsel Nikhel Sus said Tuesday the group intends to keep pressing for “transparency” about DOGE.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to decide if DOGE records will stay hidden
sources.text:
Supreme Court to decide if DOGE records will stay hidden
The Supreme Court said Tuesday that it will take up an appeal from the Trump administration to block information about the so-called Department of Government Efficiency from public records requests.
The watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) sued the government in February 2025 to compel DOGE and the Office of Management and Budget to release documents related to the mass firings of federal workers during the early days of the second Trump administration.
OMB said it would respond to some Freedom of Information Act requests, but DOGE refused, claiming that it wasn’t an agency and therefore not subject to federal records law.
Judge Christopher Cooper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled in March 2025 that DOGE was likely subject to FOIA and directed the Elon Musk-led group to process CREW’s records requests on an expedited basis.
Cooper cited three factors in his ruling: executive orders that seemed to “endow USDS with substantial authority independent of the President,” statements made by Musk and President Donald Trump that pointed to that authority, and DOGE moves that exercised power over “vast swaths of the federal government.”
The Department of Justice quickly moved to block Cooper’s subsequent order for expedited discovery by submitting a writ of mandamus, “an extraordinary remedy,” according to the agency, “which should only be used in exceptional circumstances of peculiar emergency or public importance.”
In May 2025, the Supreme Court sided with the DOJ, staying the discovery schedule Cooper ordered and allowing the Trump administration to continue withholding DOGE-related documents from the public. The high court’s decision also prevented CREW from deposing Amy Gleason, DOGE’s then-acting administrator and a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services official.
Much has changed with DOGE since SCOTUS placed a stay on the proceedings. The tech collective has essentially become “institutionalized” across the federal government, with dozens of allies stationed at various agencies and other alums venturing into the private sector and reportedly cashing in on their whirlwind government destruction.
The high court’s ruling on the case will likely come next summer.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to hear case testing powers of Elon Musk DOGE investigation
sources.text:
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear an appeal by the Trump administration in a fight over access to records from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
The case stems from Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), a nonprofit organization that has sought records related to DOGE, the entity that slashed federal spending at the start of Trump’s second term.
Supporters of DOGE, which was led by Elon Musk, viewed the department as saving taxpayer funds by eliminating duplicative, outdated or inefficient federal functions. Critics raised concerns about DOGE's scope and intent, worrying it was used to justify deep cuts to useful social programs, environmental protections or scientific agencies under the banner of “efficiency.”
CREW has argued that DOGE is a federal agency and therefore subject to FOIA requests, but the Trump administration has said it is a presidential advisory body and exempt from FOIA requirements.
Earlier, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper authorized CREW’s discovery requests into DOGE. But in June 2025, the Supreme Court decided that he ruled too broadly and sent the case back to lower courts. It did not decide whether DOGE is subject to FOIA.
CREW then adjusted its discovery requests. DOGE has returned to the Supreme Court, arguing that the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals has continued approving “intrusive” discovery against the entity. CREW said the justices should not have picked up the case and that it followed the Court’s instructions.
The Supreme Court is now taking up the case on its merits, rather than an emergency procedural dispute.
Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told Newsweek that DOGE seemed like a “one-off” that “fizzled out” in the early days of the Trump administration, casting doubt that a Court ruling would have broader implications for future cases.
“I don’t think it’ll have broad implications in terms of discovery requests to federal agencies because those agencies are authorized by Congress. They receive funds. The heads of those agencies—they make decisions, so I really think this is more of a one-off,” he said.
CREW’s Chief Legal Counsel Nikhel Sus told Newsweek that the group “will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration's efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government."
"The lower courts have uniformly ruled that CREW is entitled to discovery in this case to help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to FOIA,” Sus said.
Newsweek also reached out to the Department of Justice via email for comment.
What Will the Supreme Court Decide?
The Supreme Court was asked to address two issues: First, whether the Court of Appeals “departed from this Court’s instructions and the separation-of-powers principles that this Court articulated in Cheney v. United States District Court.”
The second is whether a court “may order broad discovery against an Executive Office advisory body—potentially providing much information sought on the merits of a plaintiff’s FOIA claims—to determine whether FOIA’s disclosure requirements apply in the first place.”
What the Trump Administration Is Arguing
In a petition for a writ of certiorari, the Department of Justice (DOJ) wrote that the case “presents important questions about whether, and to what extent, discovery targeting a body within the Executive Office of the President can proceed for the paradoxical purpose of determining whether the [FOIA] applies to that body at all.”
The DOJ said that a discovery request made by CREW would “perversely give respondent much of the information that it sought in its actual FOIA requests (and in some respects even more) —before any court has held that FOIA applies.”
“Yet the D.C. Circuit declined to address whether any aspects of that discovery presented separation-of-powers concerns,” the DOJ wrote. “And the court declined to otherwise narrow that discovery to address this Court’s conclusion that the ‘ability to persuade’ is irrelevant to whether a body is an ‘agency’ under FOIA.”
The DOJ wrote that review is warranted for separation-of-powers reasons, arguing that it views DOGE as a body that advises the president and that the appeals court’s approval of “intrusive discovery” to assess whether FOIA applies “cannot be reconciled with FOIA.”
“This Court’s prior order rejected the premise underlying the discovery order by holding that USDS’s influence is irrelevant to FOIA’s applicability,” the DOJ said, referring to the United States Digital Service.
How CREW Responded
CREW has criticized the government’s argument that DOGE is advisory, pointing to a district court ruling that DOGE wields “substantial independent authority.”
“Undisputed facts in the public record—including the President’s statements—confirmed that USDS was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government,” CREW said. “The district court found that the other preliminary-injunction factors also supported an order directing USDS to process CREW’s FOIA request on an expedited basis.”
It argued the Supreme Court should not have taken up the case.
“The petition principally pleads for summary reversal or certiorari on the scope of the discovery order that remains after remand. But the D.C. Circuit followed this Court’s instructions on that fact-intensive question to the letter,” CREW wrote.
It said the administration “fares no better in requesting certiorari so this Court can change FOIA law by prohibiting all discovery—in every case—into the nature of an EOP entity’s authority.”
The government’s proposed rule is “impossible to square with statutory text, and it would be ripe for abuse,” CREW wrote.
“Indeed, it would allow the executive to establish hugely consequential entities like USDS, while sidestepping an important sunshine law, simply by placing those entities in EOP and obscuring the precise nature of their delegated authority."
What Happens Next
Arguments are likely to be heard later in the Supreme Court’s new term, and a decision would likely be handed down sometime next year.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jenni Fink and Sam Wilson.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to review dispute over access to DOGE records
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court announced Tuesday that it would review a long-running dispute over how much information the Department of Government Efficiency formed by Elon Musk must disclose in response to public records requests.
In the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term, Musk’s initiative, known as DOGE, swept through federal agencies seeking to overhaul the government bureaucracy and fire scores of workers. Musk eventually departed last year amid declining influence and friction with the president and after failing to deliver on promised cuts to the budget.
But a nonprofit watchdog group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, has continued to press for information about the entity’s operations. The group known as CREW had filed an expedited request for records under the Freedom of Information Act. After it did not receive the records, the group filed a lawsuit, saying DOGE had violated public records laws.
The justices are expected to schedule the matter for oral arguments early next year and to issue a decision in the case before their new term ends in late June or early July. It is one of several cases before the Supreme Court testing the Trump administration’s policies.
At issue in the case will be whether the quasi-private entity is similar to other federal agencies, which are generally subject to federal public records laws. The administration has argued it is instead more like presidential advisory groups, which are able to keep more information private.
A federal judge in Washington, Christopher R. Cooper, concluded last year that Musk’s group was likely subject to the records law and ordered it to turn over the documents during the lawsuit discovery process. A three-judge panel on a federal appeals court agreed.
The case previously reached the Supreme Court on a temporary and emergency basis last year. In June 2025, the justices paused CREW’s discovery request, blocking the group from getting DOGE’s records and sending the case back to the lower courts for more litigation and discussion over how to narrow the set of records that Musk’s group was required to turn over.
The justices at that time were divided along ideological lines, with the conservative majority saying that “separation of powers concerns counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal executive branch communications.”
The three liberal justices noted their dissent. The new case will resolve the legal issues in a more lasting way.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Takes Up President Trump’s Fight Over DOGE Records – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Jack
sources.text:
President Trump’s administration is taking its fight over DOGE records back to the Supreme Court. The justices agreed Tuesday to hear an appeal challenging court-ordered access to the inner workings of the government-cutting operation once associated with Elon Musk.
The fight reaches a basic question about presidential power: how much can a court demand from White House advisers before deciding whether the public-records law covers their office at all?
Musk has left government service, but the legal battle has outlasted his Washington assignment. Tuesday’s action puts the administration’s objections before the justices for a full review.
The new order puts the dispute over court-ordered access to DOGE’s operations on the justices’ agenda:
NEW: The Supreme Court agreed to hear the Trump administration's challenge to court-ordered discovery into DOGE's operations in a lawsuit over whether it must comply with federal public records laws. pic.twitter.com/KNloL8ZtPK
— SCOTUS Wire (@scotus_wire) October 13, 2026
In its petition, the Justice Department describes a dispute over the U.S. DOGE Service, an office within the Executive Office of the President. The administration argues that its advisory role places it outside the Freedom of Information Act’s requirements for federal agencies.
Government lawyers object to discovery requests covering staff information, internal directives and plans to access classified information. They also challenge a deposition of DOGE administrator Amy Gleason concerning the operation’s structure and responsibilities.
The administration says those demands could hand over much of the information the lawsuit seeks before the court settles whether FOIA applies. It argues that discovery itself can intrude on protected executive-branch deliberations.
The petition also faults the appeals court’s handling of earlier instructions to narrow the requests. Solicitor General Sauer is asking the justices to enforce limits grounded in the separation of powers.
That is a serious concern even beyond DOGE. A president needs room to hear advice, weigh proposals and reject bad ideas without every internal exchange becoming material for a lawsuit.
But the strength of that argument depends on what the office actually does. Giving advice and exercising government authority are different jobs.
The objection is that compulsory disclosure could defeat the advisory structure before its legal protections are resolved:
Rather than apply settled law, the district court ordered discovery — documents and depositions — into whether @DOGE is subject to FOIA.
Discovery would have defeated the entire point of the above structure, providing intrusive, harassing disclosures by other means. 5/
— James Burnham (@BurnhamDC) October 13, 2026
The group seeking the records, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, argues in its opposition brief that DOGE exercised substantial independent authority. It says the office’s actions and structure justify treating it as an agency subject to FOIA.
CREW points to the executive orders establishing DOGE and to public statements about its role across the government. It disputes the administration’s characterization of the central office as a body that merely advised the president.
The group also says it withdrew requests about DOGE’s recommendations after the justices intervened in June 2025. In its account, the remaining discovery addresses the office’s structure and authority, and the appeals court followed the instructions it received.
CREW urged the justices to reject the appeal, warning that an overly broad exemption could let an administration place powerful operations inside the president’s office and shield them from the records law.
The court must draw a workable boundary around presidential advice while preserving the records obligations Congress imposed on actual agencies. Even the process of gathering evidence can cross that boundary, according to the administration.
The two questions presented focus on separation of powers and whether discovery can precede a decision that FOIA applies:
The Court just granted cert in US DOGE Service, which asks whether (1) COA departed from the separation-of-powers principles in Cheney v. District Court; (2) Whether a ct can order discovery against an Exec Office advisory body to decide if FOIA's disclosure requirements apply

sources.text:
Justices will examine whether a watchdog can obtain information about Musk’s government-cutting initiative.
The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear the Trump administration’s challenge to a court order requiring disclosure of information about Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, setting up a consequential legal battle over government transparency and presidential authority.
The justices will review a dispute involving Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog organization seeking records about DOGE’s structure, operations, and role in the sweeping federal workforce reductions carried out during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The administration argues that DOGE was a presidential advisory organization exempt from the Freedom of Information Act, while the watchdog maintains that the initiative exercised powers normally associated with a federal agency.
The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in early 2027 and issue a decision by the end of June.
Supreme Court agrees to hear administration’s appeal
The case, U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, stems from a lawsuit filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, commonly known as CREW.
The watchdog organization submitted a public records request in early 2025 seeking information about DOGE’s organization and activities.
Its requests included records concerning the initiative’s organizational structure, financial disclosures, and involvement in decisions affecting federal agencies.
The administration refused to process the request, arguing that DOGE was housed within the Executive Office of the President and served an advisory function.
FOIA generally requires federal agencies to make qualifying records available to the public, subject to statutory exemptions.
But the law does not apply in the same way to the president’s immediate personal staff or units whose sole function is advising and assisting the president.
The government contends that DOGE belongs in the latter category.
Trump administration invokes presidential confidentiality
The Justice Department has warned that allowing the watchdog to examine DOGE’s internal operations would interfere with presidential confidentiality.
In its Supreme Court filing, the administration argued that the lower courts had authorized an excessively intrusive inquiry into the workings of presidential advisers.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the ruling threatened the “autonomy and confidentiality” of those advisers.
The administration also warned that the decision could encourage similar lawsuits against future presidents.
According to its filing, the dispute extends beyond the records CREW initially requested.
The government objects to a lower court’s authorization of discovery, the legal process through which parties obtain evidence during litigation.
The process would require DOGE to produce internal documents and likely make senior officials available for questioning under oath.
The administration maintains that those demands are inappropriate before the judicial branch conclusively determines whether DOGE is subject to FOIA.
Watchdog says DOGE exercised independent power
CREW disputes the administration’s description of DOGE as a purely advisory organization.
The watchdog argues that DOGE personnel helped direct significant changes across the federal government.
Those activities included canceling contracts, reducing the federal workforce, and obtaining access to sensitive government information systems.
CREW maintains that such actions went beyond providing advice to the president.
In a Supreme Court filing, the organization argued that the public record showed DOGE was exercising “enormous independent authority across the federal government.”
The group says information about DOGE’s actual responsibilities is necessary to determine whether it qualifies as a federal agency under FOIA.
If DOGE exercised independent governmental authority, courts could conclude that at least some of its records fall within federal disclosure requirements.
If it functioned solely as an advisory body, the administration’s argument for excluding it from FOIA would be stronger.
Federal judge initially sided with watchdog
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in April 2025 that CREW had demonstrated a sufficient basis for obtaining information about DOGE’s structure and responsibilities.
The judge found that DOGE likely qualified as an agency subject to FOIA.
He ordered expedited processing of the watchdog’s records request and authorized limited discovery to help resolve the dispute.
Discovery included questioning Amy Gleason, DOGE’s acting administrator.
The administration challenged the order, arguing that the inquiry would expose confidential communications within the executive branch.
The dispute reached the Supreme Court in June 2025.
In a 6-3 decision, the justices set aside the lower court’s discovery order and directed further consideration of the separation-of-powers concerns raised by the government.
The majority concluded that portions of the order were too broad.
The Court specifically questioned demands that could reveal internal recommendations made by DOGE personnel and whether executive branch officials followed those recommendations.
Supreme Court previously limited disclosure
The June 2025 ruling did not conclusively resolve whether DOGE was subject to FOIA.
Instead, the justices directed the lower courts to narrow the discovery process.
The Supreme Court emphasized the need for judicial restraint when litigation involves internal executive branch communications.
After the ruling, CREW reduced the scope of the information it sought.
The organization abandoned certain requests concerning internal recommendations and focused on DOGE’s organizational structure and the extent of its authority.
Its revised requests sought information about directives involving federal contracts, workforce reductions, and access to sensitive agency systems.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit subsequently allowed the narrower discovery process to proceed.
The appeals court concluded that the revised requests complied with the Supreme Court’s instructions.
The Trump administration disagreed and returned to the high court.
Tuesday’s decision to hear the appeal marks the Supreme Court’s second intervention in the case.
Administration objects to questioning DOGE official
One of the most contested aspects of the case involves the proposed deposition of Gleason.
A deposition allows attorneys to question a witness under oath as part of the evidence-gathering process.
CREW argues that questioning the DOGE administrator would help establish whether the organization independently exercised governmental authority.
The administration contends that the deposition would intrude into the operations of presidential advisers.
Its attorneys argue that permitting such questioning before resolving DOGE’s legal status could undermine protections afforded to the executive branch.
The government has also warned that a ruling against it could establish a precedent for using FOIA litigation to obtain information about presidential advisers who ordinarily would not be subject to the statute.
CREW counters that the administration cannot avoid scrutiny merely by describing an organization as advisory if its personnel actually exercised independent governmental powers.
The Supreme Court’s eventual decision could clarify how courts should investigate that distinction.
Musk-led initiative reshaped federal agencies
DOGE became one of the most prominent initiatives of Trump’s second administration.
The president established the effort shortly after returning to the White House in January 2025, promising to reduce federal spending, eliminate waste, and shrink the federal bureaucracy.
Musk, the billionaire entrepreneur behind Tesla and SpaceX, served as the initiative’s most visible leader during its early months.
DOGE personnel were assigned to agencies throughout the executive branch.
The initiative participated in efforts to reduce staffing, cancel government contracts, and restructure federal programs.
Its activities also generated controversy over access to sensitive government databases.
Those included systems maintained by the Internal Revenue Service, Social Security Administration, and Office of Personnel Management.
Supporters argued that the initiative was necessary to identify waste and reduce unnecessary spending.
Critics questioned the legality, accuracy, and consequences of some of its actions.
Musk left his government role in May 2025.
Federal workforce reductions remain under scrutiny
DOGE’s campaign to reduce government employment had substantial consequences for federal agencies and workers.
The initiative promoted voluntary separation programs and other measures designed to reduce payroll costs.
The Government Accountability Office subsequently examined costs associated with administrative leave during the administration’s workforce restructuring.
According to a GAO analysis, federal administrative leave costs reached approximately $9.5 billion in 2025, compared with substantially lower costs in 2023.
The agency attributed approximately $6.7 billion of the 2025 total to employees who accepted a buyout offer associated with the administration’s workforce reduction initiative.
Those findings provide context for the broader debate over DOGE’s effectiveness and costs.
They do not determine whether DOGE qualifies as a federal agency under FOIA.
Government transparency at center of dispute
The Freedom of Information Act is intended to provide public access to records held by federal agencies.
Congress enacted the law in 1966, and it has since become a principal mechanism through which journalists, researchers, watchdog organizations, and private citizens obtain government information.
Federal agencies may withhold records under specified exemptions, including protections involving national security, personal privacy, and certain privileged communications.
The current dispute presents a threshold question: whether DOGE falls within the category of organizations required to respond to FOIA requests.
CREW argues that allowing an organization to exercise substantial governmental authority while avoiding disclosure obligations would undermine the law’s transparency purpose.
The administration argues that forcing presidential advisers to disclose internal information would interfere with the president’s ability to receive confidential advice.
Both positions involve established legal principles.
The Supreme Court must determine how those principles apply to DOGE’s particular structure and activities.
Justices could clarify limits of executive privilege
The case could affect more than DOGE.
Presidents frequently rely on offices, councils, and advisers within the Executive Office of the President.
Some perform primarily advisory functions, while others exercise authority established by statute or delegated through executive action.
The distinction determines whether those entities are subject to public records laws.
A Supreme Court ruling could clarify what evidence courts may examine when deciding whether a White House entity operates as an agency.
It could also establish limits on the discovery available to plaintiffs seeking to challenge an administration’s characterization of its own organizations.
The Court may choose to address the scope of permissible discovery without definitively deciding DOGE’s FOIA status.
The exact reach of its eventual decision will depend on the questions the justices resolve.
Decision expected by summer 2027
The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled oral arguments.
The case is expected to be heard during the Court’s current term, with a ruling likely by late June 2027.
Until then, the dispute over access to DOGE records remains unresolved.
The justices’ decision to hear the administration’s appeal does not establish that the government acted unlawfully by withholding information.
Nor does it establish that DOGE is permanently exempt from public records requirements.
The immediate legal question concerns whether lower courts can require additional evidence about DOGE’s structure and authority while determining the organization’s status under FOIA.
The broader stakes involve the extent to which a presidential initiative that helped direct major changes across the federal government must disclose how it operated.
For the Trump administration, the case concerns the confidentiality of presidential advisers.
For CREW, it concerns the public’s ability to examine the actions of an organization that played a major role in reshaping federal operations.
The Supreme Court will now decide how far that examination can proceed.

The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to hear the Trump administration’s latest challenge involving the United States DOGE Service, potentially shielding presidential advisers from a lower-court discovery order.
U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia appeared first among the cases granted review in the Supreme Court’s Tuesday orders.
In a petition filed in March, Solicitor General D. John Sauer—who previously served as President Donald Trump’s personal attorney—accused U.S. District Judge Christopher “Casey” Cooper and the D.C. Circuit of authorizing “wide-ranging and intrusive discovery” into Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. Sauer argued that DOGE is part of the Executive Office of the President and exists to advise the president.
Cooper, an Obama appointee overseeing the Kennedy Center dispute, ruled for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington and allowed the group to pursue expedited discovery. The judge also rejected the administration’s claim that DOGE is not an agency covered by the Freedom of Information Act.
The Justice Department told the Supreme Court that it had already sought the justices’ intervention, secured a stay and obtained a “limited narrowing of the discovery.” But the department said the D.C. Circuit continued approving what it called invasive requests involving a presidential advisory body, without properly weighing separation-of-powers concerns, FOIA’s requirements or the Supreme Court’s earlier order.
RELATED: Missing Air Force General’s UFO Links Fuel Fresh Allegations
The administration presented the justices with two questions, grounding its arguments in the “critical separation of powers principles” the Supreme Court outlined in a 2004 decision involving then-Vice President Dick Cheney:
1. Whether the appeals court’s ruling conflicted with the Supreme Court’s instructions and the separation-of-powers standards established in Cheney v. United States District Court, 542 U.S. 367 (2004).
2. Whether a court can require extensive discovery from an advisory body within the Executive Office of the President—potentially revealing information central to the substance of a plaintiff’s FOIA case—in order to decide whether FOIA applies to that body at all.
The Trump administration maintained that the inner workings of a presidential advisory body, particularly its most sensitive operations, should remain protected. It argued that Judge Cooper’s discovery order—not DOGE’s conduct—should be the focus of the Supreme Court’s review.
“The Court could either grant plenary review of both the separation-of-powers issues concerning discovery into part of the Executive Office of the President and the statutory question of how to tell whether a body counts as an ‘agency’ for FOIA purposes,” the Justice Department wrote. “Or the Court could summarily reverse on the separation-of-powers issue alone because the order below so seriously departs from Cheney’s principles.”

The Supreme Court will decide whether a federal judge exceeded judicial authority by ordering access to internal Department of Government Efficiency communications, setting up a significant dispute over executive branch confidentiality and public records laws.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The U.S. Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to review the Trump administration’s challenge to a federal court order requiring the Department of Government Efficiency to produce internal communications and other evidence in a public records lawsuit, placing the limits of judicial oversight of presidential advisers before the nation’s highest court.
The justices granted the administration’s petition in U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, a case arising from a Freedom of Information Act dispute involving the government watchdog organization Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, commonly known as CREW. The organization is seeking records that could reveal how DOGE exercised influence over federal spending, staffing and government operations during President Donald Trump’s second term.
The Supreme Court’s October 13 order granted review without providing an explanation or recording any dissenting votes. The justices have not scheduled oral arguments, although the case is expected to be heard in early 2027, with a decision potentially arriving before the court concludes its term next summer.
At issue is whether a federal judge can compel extensive evidence-gathering from an executive branch office to determine whether that same office is subject to federal public records requirements. The administration argues that the disputed order intrudes into confidential presidential advisory activities, while CREW maintains that access to the evidence is necessary to establish whether DOGE exercised powers that make it legally accountable under FOIA.
The dispute does not directly concern whether DOGE’s spending reductions, personnel decisions or broader government restructuring initiatives were lawful. Instead, it centers on the legal status of the organization and how much information courts can require the administration to provide while deciding whether the public has a right to obtain its records.
The litigation began after Trump established DOGE through an executive order on January 20, 2025, assigning the initiative responsibility for advancing government efficiency, reducing administrative costs and modernizing federal operations. Tech entrepreneur Elon Musk became the initiative’s most prominent leader before leaving his government role in May 2025.
DOGE rapidly became involved in efforts to reduce federal spending, eliminate government positions, examine agency operations and identify programs for restructuring or termination. Its activities prompted legal challenges from employees, labor organizations, nonprofit groups and government accountability advocates seeking information about how its decisions were made.
CREW filed its lawsuit in early 2025 after requesting organizational records, financial disclosures and other documents related to DOGE’s operations. The watchdog group argued that the organization functioned as a federal agency and should therefore be required to comply with the Freedom of Information Act.
The Trump administration disputed that characterization, maintaining that DOGE was an advisory body operating within the Executive Office of the President rather than an independent federal agency subject to routine public records disclosure.
That distinction is central to the case because FOIA generally requires covered federal agencies to disclose records upon request, subject to statutory exemptions. Presidential advisers whose responsibilities are limited to assisting the president may fall outside the law’s definition of an agency.
The question becomes more complicated when an executive office does more than provide advice and instead exercises independent operational authority over government programs or personnel.
CREW contends that DOGE’s substantial involvement in federal agency operations demonstrates that its responsibilities extended beyond providing recommendations to the president. The organization argues that the public should be able to examine documents explaining how DOGE participated in decisions affecting government employees, spending and federal services.
The administration maintains that the office operated under presidential direction and that subjecting its internal deliberations to broad discovery would interfere with the executive branch’s ability to obtain confidential advice.
The legal dispute reached U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington, who permitted CREW to seek evidence concerning DOGE’s structure, responsibilities and activities.
Cooper authorized discovery intended to help determine whether DOGE possessed sufficient independent authority to qualify as an agency under FOIA. The order required production of certain documents and contemplated testimony from DOGE’s acting administrator, Amy Gleason.
Discovery is the formal process through which parties in litigation obtain documents, testimony and other evidence relevant to disputed factual or legal issues. Although commonly used in civil cases, discovery involving presidential advisers can raise additional concerns about confidentiality and the separation of powers.
The administration objected to the scope of Cooper’s order, arguing that it would compel the disclosure of internal presidential communications before the court had established that DOGE was legally subject to FOIA.
Government attorneys sought intervention from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, asking the appellate court to block the discovery requirements through a writ of mandamus, an extraordinary form of judicial relief available under limited circumstances.
After the appeals court declined to halt the proceedings, the administration turned to the Supreme Court.
The justices previously intervened in May 2025, directing the appeals court to reconsider the discovery order in light of constitutional concerns involving the separation of powers.
The Supreme Court’s earlier action did not resolve whether DOGE was subject to FOIA. Instead, it instructed the lower court to examine whether the requested discovery could be narrowed to reduce potential interference with presidential advisory functions.
CREW subsequently withdrew several requests, reducing the scope of the information it sought. However, the remaining discovery demands continued to include internal communications and proposed testimony from DOGE’s leadership.
The D.C. Circuit again declined to issue the requested writ of mandamus, leaving the administration dissatisfied with the extent of the lower court’s review.
In its petition asking the Supreme Court to intervene, the Justice Department characterized the district court’s requirements as an unusually broad intrusion into executive branch deliberations.
The administration argued that the appeals court failed to adequately implement the Supreme Court’s previous instructions to narrow discovery and give proper consideration to the constitutional protections afforded to presidential advisers.
Government lawyers also questioned whether courts should permit extensive discovery into an executive advisory body’s activities before determining that the organization is subject to FOIA.
The administration maintains that allowing such proceedings could effectively grant plaintiffs access to sensitive information they might not otherwise be entitled to obtain through the public records law.
Its position rests partly on the principle that the president must be able to receive candid advice from senior officials without exposing every internal conversation to litigation-driven disclosure.
Courts have previously recognized that some communications involving presidential decision-making deserve special protection. The boundaries of those protections, however, depend on the nature of the information requested, the legal claims involved and the responsibilities of the officials participating in the discussions.
CREW argues that the administration’s position would make it difficult to determine whether an organization exercising substantial government authority is subject to transparency requirements.
The watchdog group maintains that courts must be able to examine the actual activities of an executive office rather than simply accept the administration’s description of its legal status.
In its filing opposing Supreme Court review, CREW argued that the government had not demonstrated the extraordinary circumstances necessary to justify mandamus relief.
The organization also disputed the administration’s portrayal of DOGE as merely advisory, pointing to evidence developed in other litigation concerning the organization’s involvement in federal operations.
CREW contended that the government had previously acknowledged that some discovery could be appropriate to determine whether an entity within the Executive Office of the President qualifies as an agency.
The disagreement therefore concerns both the permissible scope of evidence-gathering and the legal standards for intervening in a lower court’s management of discovery.
The Supreme Court’s decision to hear the case establishes an opportunity to clarify those standards in litigation involving presidential advisers and federal public records requests.
The justices could determine that the lower courts authorized discovery that was too broad, establish additional limits on such requests or conclude that the existing procedures adequately protected executive branch interests.
Their eventual ruling could also influence how lower courts approach future cases involving offices whose responsibilities combine presidential advice with substantial participation in federal agency operations.
The Freedom of Information Act, enacted in 1966, was designed to improve public access to federal government records. It generally permits individuals and organizations to request agency documents without demonstrating a personal interest in the information.
Federal agencies may withhold certain records under statutory exemptions covering matters such as national security, personal privacy, law enforcement investigations and privileged internal communications.
The statute does not automatically apply to every office associated with the presidency. Courts have distinguished between federal agencies and presidential staff whose primary responsibilities involve advising and assisting the president.
That distinction reflects constitutional considerations arising from the separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers.
Congress established public records requirements for executive agencies, while the courts have recognized that the president and certain immediate advisers require confidentiality to carry out constitutional responsibilities.
Determining whether an office falls within FOIA can depend on how it operates in practice, including whether its officials possess independent authority to make decisions affecting federal programs.
The DOGE dispute tests that framework because the organization was formally placed within the Executive Office of the President while participating in activities that extended across numerous federal agencies.
Its initiatives included reviewing agency spending, examining information technology systems, identifying programs for reductions and working with government officials on staffing and organizational changes.
Those activities have made DOGE’s institutional status a significant legal question in several proceedings.
CREW argues that the organization’s involvement in consequential government decisions supports treating it as an agency subject to public disclosure requirements.
The administration maintains that DOGE’s actions occurred within a structure of presidential supervision and coordination with established federal agencies.
The Supreme Court is not being asked to determine the full merits of those competing characterizations at this stage. The immediate question concerns whether the district court had sufficient authority to compel the disputed evidence while evaluating DOGE’s legal classification.
The distinction is important because a ruling limiting discovery would not necessarily establish that DOGE is exempt from FOIA in every circumstance.
Likewise, a ruling allowing discovery would not automatically require the administration to release all DOGE documents to the public.
Additional proceedings could be necessary to determine whether the organization qualifies as an agency and, if it does, which specific records must be disclosed under the statute.
The controversy has broader implications for government transparency because presidential administrations frequently establish offices, task forces and advisory bodies to coordinate policy initiatives.
Some entities operate primarily as internal advisory organizations, while others may take on responsibilities that resemble those of traditional executive agencies.
How courts distinguish between those functions can affect public access to records documenting federal decision-making.
The administration’s concern is that extensive discovery could undermine the confidentiality of presidential deliberations even when an office is ultimately found to be outside FOIA.
CREW’s concern is that denying access to evidence about an organization’s actual authority could allow significant government activities to escape statutory transparency requirements.
The case also arrives amid continuing scrutiny of DOGE’s record during its first year.
The organization promoted efforts to reduce spending and reshape federal operations, while critics questioned the accuracy of some claimed savings and the effects of government workforce reductions.
Federal auditors and outside researchers have challenged portions of DOGE’s reported savings, including whether certain claimed reductions represented actual budgetary savings.
Those disputes form part of the political and administrative background to the litigation, but the Supreme Court’s review will focus on the discovery order and the legal protections surrounding executive branch communications.
The justices’ decision to grant review does not indicate how they will ultimately rule.
Supreme Court orders accepting cases ordinarily provide little explanation, and Tuesday’s announcement included no separate opinions.
The court’s public docket for the dispute identifies the matter as U.S. DOGE Service, et al. v. United States District Court for the District of Columbia, et al. and records the administration’s efforts to obtain appellate intervention after the lower courts permitted discovery to proceed.
The Justice Department filed its petition in March 2026, following the D.C. Circuit’s July 2025 decision and its subsequent denial of rehearing in December.
CREW submitted its opposition in June 2026, and the justices considered the petition before granting review Tuesday.
The case is expected to move forward through written briefs and oral arguments during the court’s current term, with a decision anticipated by summer 2027.
Until then, the litigation leaves unresolved whether the government must comply with the contested discovery requirements and whether DOGE’s operational role brings it within the scope of federal public records law.
The Supreme Court’s eventual decision could shape how much evidence courts may demand from presidential advisory organizations when members of the public seek to determine whether those organizations are exercising authority subject to federal transparency laws.
For the Trump administration, the case presents an opportunity to establish stronger limits on judicial inquiries into internal executive branch communications. For CREW, it concerns the ability to obtain information necessary to determine whether an influential government office must comply with FOIA.
Tuesday’s action places those competing principles before the Supreme Court, setting up a major legal examination of government accountability, presidential confidentiality and the boundaries of judicial oversight.

sources.news_title: Court grants cases on DOGE data dispute, prisoners’ rights, and what qualifies as “material support” for terrorism
sources.text:
Updated on Oct. 13 at 2:29 p.m. EDT
The Supreme Court on Tuesday added three new cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, agreeing to decide, among other things, what kinds of orders trial courts can issue in disputes over access to government information and whether working as a cook in a camp run by violent separatists qualifies as providing “material support” for terrorism under federal immigration law.
President Donald Trump created the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE, in January 2025 to advance his agenda by “modernizing Federal technology and software to maximize governmental efficiency and productivity.” Although it is not a cabinet-level department, DOGE was widely involved in Trump’s efforts to reduce the size of the federal government.
The dispute now before the court, U.S. Doge Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, began after a government watchdog group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act for (among other things) communications between the DOGE administrator, Amy Gleason, and DOGE staff, as well as financial disclosures submitted by DOGE personnel.
CREW went to federal court in Washington last year, asking DOGE to disclose documents that it said it wanted before Congress passed a bill to fund the federal government.
CREW also sought to fast-track discovery – the process of exchanging information in litigation – to determine whether DOGE is a federal “agency” that must comply with FOIA. It asked for a list of current and former DOGE employees, a list of employees and positions for which DOGE had recommended termination, a list of government contracts and grants that DOGE had recommended be canceled, and the opportunity to depose Gleason.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper granted most of CREW’s discovery requests, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit turned down DOGE’s plea to pause that order.
U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer then came to the Supreme Court in May 2025, asking the justices to intervene. He told the justices that the discovery required under Cooper’s order “offends the separation of powers by compromising the ‘necessity’ for confidentiality that allows presidential advisors to provide ‘candid, objective’ advice and communication.”
In a two-page, unsigned order in early June 2025, the court – over the objections of Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson – sent the dispute back to the D.C. Circuit for another look. The majority wrote that the portions of Cooper’s discovery order that required the government to disclose the content of DOGE’s recommendations within the executive branch, as well as whether those recommendations were followed, were too broad. Moreover, it added, concerns about the separation of powers between the branches of government “counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal Executive Branch communications.” The court put Cooper’s discovery orders on hold while the litigation continued.
When the case returned to the lower courts, CREW modified its discovery requests so that it no longer sought information about “recommendations” made by U.S. DOGE employees. The lower courts then declined to block CREW’s requests.
DOGE came to the Supreme Court in March, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that the D.C. Circuit “has continued to approve intrusive discovery against a presidential advisory body without adequate consideration for the separation of powers, the FOIA statute, and” the Supreme Court’s order last year on the interim docket. Among other things, he argued, that order “required the courts below to reassess all remaining discovery—not just requests for USDS recommendations—with the ‘deference and restraint’ applicable to presidential advisors under Cheney v. U.S. District Court,” a 2004 case in which the justices held that when considering requests for information directed at the vice-president and other senior executive branch officials, “special considerations” should “control when the Executive Branch’s interests in maintaining the autonomy of its office and safeguarding the confidentiality of its communications are implicated.”
CREW urged the justices to deny review. It argued that in formulating the new discovery order, the D.C. Circuit had “followed this Court’s instructions” in its earlier ruling on the interim docket “to the letter.” Instead, it contended, the government was seeking “to transform this Court’s carefully crafted stay-stage order into a sweeping ruling that Cheney effectively forecloses discovery in this case. That is not what this Court said,” CREW insisted, “and, especially after remand, this case looks nothing like Cheney.”
On Tuesday, the court agreed to address the D.C. Circuit’s ruling.
The immigration case granted on Tuesday, Blanche v. Ozurumba, was also brought to the court by the Trump administration. In a petition for review filed in May, Sauer asked the justices to clarify what type of support an immigrant must be shown to have provided to a terrorist organization in order to be “removable and ineligible for various immigration benefits” under a federal immigration law that states that an individual who “affords material support” to such a group is “ineligible to be admitted to the United States.”
Blanche v. Ozurumba involves Izuchukwu Ozurumba, “a native and citizen of Nigeria,” who worked as a cook in a camp run by a separatist organization known as the “Unknown Gunmen” “for about six months” before escaping, according to the government’s petition. He made his way to Venezuela and then the United States, where he applied for asylum, but an immigration judge and then the Board of Immigration Appeals concluded that his work in the camp amounted to “material support” for terrorism and that he was, therefore, ineligible for asylum.
Ozurumba appealed his case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, which held that “the record does not support the conclusion that Ozurumba provided material support” to the Unknown Gunmen. “Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have ‘sustained’ the organization in the broadest possible sense—by converting raw groceries into meals they enjoyed—but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” concluded 4th Circuit Judge James Wynn in the majority opinion.
The Supreme Court will clarify what qualifies as "material support" of a terrorist organization such that an immigrant is ineligible for asylum and removable from the United States.
The justices also granted review on Tuesday in Berry v. United States, on whether a certificate of appealability – a prerequisite for appealing a decision that denies a request for post-conviction relief – may be granted to a prisoner whose claim is foreclosed by his own circuit’s precedent but would be allowed to proceed in a different circuit. In his petition for review, Corey Berry emphasized that the federal courts of appeals were split over this question on circuit splits.
The court on Tuesday declined to take up the case of Jesus Herrera-Salazar, who was sentenced to 15 months in prison, followed by two years of supervised release, after he pleaded guilty to being “found in” the United States after having been deported. While on supervised release, Herrera-Salazar was instructed not to leave eastern Oklahoma; after he was pulled over in a traffic stop there, he was again indicted and convicted on a charge of being “found in” the U.S. after having been deported. After his second conviction, he was sentenced to 21 months in prison and three years of supervised release.
Herrera-Salazar argued that the second indictment violated the Constitution’s double jeopardy clause, which provides that “[n]o person shall ... be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.” He contended that both sets of charges and convictions stemmed from the same offense – being present in the United States after deportation. After the lower courts rejected that argument, Herrera-Salazar asked the Supreme Court to weigh in.
The justices on Tuesday denied that request. Justice Sonia Sotomayor penned a statement, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, regarding the decision not to weigh in on the case. She wrote that “[b]ecause I hope the facts of this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has since been removed from the United States, I concur in the Court’s decision not to grant review in this case. I write, however, to underscore the serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar.”
“When a defendant is convicted of a crime that involves continuous, uninterrupted conduct,” Sotomayor stated, the court’s cases “and the logic of the Double Jeopardy Clause strongly suggest that the Government is barred from charging that defendant with the same continuous crime for a second time simply by focusing on a different time marker.” Otherwise, she posited, the government could bring multiple indictments against a defendant for each month of a continuous crime. “There is even more force to this double jeopardy objection,” she added, “where the Government itself effectively forbids the defendant to cease his unlawful conduct.”
The court did not act on several high-profile petitions for review, including a challenge to a Maryland suburb’s admissions policy for selecting students for magnet middle schools and a pair of challenges to the federal ban on home distilleries. The justices will consider those cases and others at their Oct. 16 conference.
Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.
Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.
