sources.news_title: Supreme Court takes up DOGE documents fight and an asylum plea from a chef for terrorists
sources.text:
Supreme Court takes up DOGE documents fight and an asylum plea from a chef for terrorists
By John Fritze, CNN
(CNN) — The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to take up a pair of appeals from President Donald Trump’s administration, including a case about the Department of Government Efficiency, the government-cutting entity once run by Elon Musk, and a dispute about a Nigerian man who was denied asylum because he once cooked meals for members of a terrorist organization.
The two cases are a reflection of Trump’s return to power last year, both his crackdown on immigration and his moves to slash government spending.
The DOGE case raises fundamental questions about the power and transparency of an entity that slashed agencies with unusual speed last year. A left-leaning watchdog, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, sued to gain access to those documents under a federal transparency law, and lower federal courts have ordered DOGE to produce information to help decide whether the law applies.
The asylum case centers on a Nigerian national who served as a cook for a separatist group carrying out terrorist attacks, a dispute that the Trump administration says could affect thousands of immigration cases annually.
What was happening at DOGE?
The Trump administration appealed lower court orders requiring DOGE to disclose records, arguing that separation of powers concerns should bar such “wide-ranging and intrusive discovery” demands from federal courts. Those orders, the Justice Department told the Supreme Court, would “perversely give respondent much of the information that it sought in its” request for documents under the Freedom of Information Act “before any court has held that FOIA applies.”
While DOGE has slipped from public view, it had a significant impact on the federal government – carrying out Trump’s promise of limiting the federal government. Central to the case is whether DOGE was exercising power on its own, which might make it subject to open records requests, or whether it was merely acting as an advisory body to the president, in which case it would likely be shielded from those requests.
The Trump administration, which the president frequently claims is the most transparent in history, has aggressively fought the case, describing DOGE as a “presidential advisory body” within the White House that is tasked “with providing recommendations” rather than making decisions.
Over the dissent of the three liberal justices, the Supreme Court last year came down on the side of DOGE in an earlier stage of the case, requiring lower courts to narrow the scope of the material ordered in discovery. CREW withdrew its request for certain documents but lower courts allowed other requests to stand. Now, the Supreme Court will decide if the more pared down requests were proper.
The lower court ordered DOGE to provide all “directives” by its administrator to its employees, to disclose any plans to access classified information and a deposition by the head of DOGE, Amy Gleason.
Guns and butter
Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who entered the United States in 2023 and later claimed asylum, says he was forced to cook at a camp for the Unknown Gunmen in Nigeria until he escaped during a run for groceries and gas. An immigration judge denied his asylum claim under a federal law that bars sanctuary for any migrant who provided “material support” to a terrorist organization.
The Supreme Court has increasingly made immigration a central theme of its new term. It is already reviewing Trump’s push to deport migrants to countries they have no connection with and his administration’s mandatory detention policies.
“Providing meals to a terrorist organization’s members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles,” US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the Trump administration’s top appellate attorney, told the Supreme Court in its appeal.
Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in 2025.
The Trump administration told the justices the particulars of Ozurumba’s case don’t matter. The law, it argued, “does not distinguish between guns and butter.”
But the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals focused on the word “material” in the law, finding that Ozurumba’s six-month stint cooking meals for the separatist group didn’t meet that threshold. Ozurumba’s lawyers said their client didn’t realize what he was getting into when he sought the job and then was forced to continue to perform it against his will.
“Under the government’s reading, seemingly any interaction with a terrorist organization could be characterized as material support,” his attorneys said. A priest who hears confession to all comers, they argue, would be viewed as providing spiritual counsel. A doctor who treats a patient affiliated with a terrorist organization, they argue, could also be punished.
“Under such a test, ‘material’ loses all meaning – every conceivable form of support, no matter how attenuated, compelled, or incidental, would suffice,” they told the justices.
Decisions in both cases are expected by next summer.

The Supreme Court on Oct. 13 agreed to decide whether a federal judge improperly ordered broad discovery against the U.S. DOGE Service in a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit that pits a watchdog group’s demand for records against the government’s claim that the order reaches too deeply into internal executive branch advice.
Discovery is part of the evidence-gathering process in litigation.
DOGE is the Department of Government Efficiency, a White House office formed in early 2025 to reduce federal spending and regulations. It was led by tech entrepreneur Elon Musk until he left in May 2025.

The group also says it withdrew requests about DOGE’s recommendations after the justices intervened in June 2025. In its account, the remaining discovery addresses the office’s structure and authority, and the appeals court followed the instructions it received.
CREW urged the justices to reject the appeal, warning that an overly broad exemption could let an administration place powerful operations inside the president’s office and shield them from the records law.
The court must draw a workable boundary around presidential advice while preserving the records obligations Congress imposed on actual agencies. Even the process of gathering evidence can cross that boundary, according to the administration.
The two questions presented focus on separation of powers and whether discovery can precede a decision that FOIA applies:
The Court just granted cert in US DOGE Service, which asks whether (1) COA departed from the separation-of-powers principles in Cheney v. District Court; (2) Whether a ct can order discovery against an Exec Office advisory body to decide if FOIA's disclosure requirements apply
— Payvand Ahdout (@PAhdout) October 13, 2026
For the administration, getting this appeal heard is a procedural advance. Tuesday’s order does not declare DOGE exempt from FOIA or decide which disputed records must ultimately be produced.
Americans deserve to know what their government is doing with their money. They also deserve courts that respect the constitutional limits on their own power.
An administration should not have to surrender disputed communications just to establish that the law protects them. The challenge for the justices is to set that limit without turning the label “adviser” into a way around disclosure obligations Congress actually imposed.
Read the full Supreme Court order here: U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court will hear DOGE transparency dispute
Supreme Court to Hear DOGE FOIA Case, Ruling Due 2027
sources.text:
The Supreme Court agreed to hear full oral arguments in the long-running fight over whether the U.S. DOGE Service has to turn over records under the Freedom of Information Act, setting up a final ruling by summer 2027 on one of the most consequential transparency disputes of Donald Trump's second term. The case, U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, will determine whether the cost-cutting unit once fronted by Elon Musk counts as a federal agency bound by public records law or an exempt presidential advisory body.
According to CBS News, the justices will hear arguments in early 2027, with a decision expected by summer of that year. It marks the second time the high court has intervened in the case, which was originally brought by the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, known as CREW. As WBAL News Radio reports, the court previously narrowed particular discovery requests, especially those involving internal recommendations, and sent the case back for further proceedings; CREW says the rest of the discovery order remained intact.
How the Legal Fight Reached the Nation's Highest Court
Cooper first ruled in CREW's favor in March 2025, finding that DOGE was likely subject to FOIA and ordering expedited processing of the group's records request, a decision detailed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington. That ruling set off a cascade of appeals from the Trump administration, which argues DOGE is exempt from FOIA as a presidential advisory body rather than an independent agency. An appeals court panel later sided with CREW again, and the Trump administration claims that panel ignored the Supreme Court's earlier direction to weigh separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on presidential advisors' autonomy and confidentiality.
Justice Department attorneys wrote that subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA's reach, per the WBAL account. The administration also says the appeals court authorized a sworn deposition of DOGE administrator Amy Gleason, according to Forbes.
The Legal Standard at the Center of the Case
Whether DOGE must comply with FOIA hinges on a specific legal test. Under federal law and the D.C. Circuit's precedent in Meyer v. Bush, entities within the Executive Office of the President are subject to FOIA only if they exercise what courts call substantial independent authority beyond simply advising and assisting the president. CREW attorneys wrote that public-record facts, including statements by the president, confirmed DOGE wielded enormous independent authority across the federal government, according to the WBAL report.
CREW narrowed its requests, and the D.C. Circuit modified the discovery order after the Supreme Court's earlier decision. DOGE itself was established through an executive order Trump signed on his first day back in office, renaming and reorganizing the U.S. Digital Service, a White House tech initiative originally created under President Barack Obama, according to Holland & Knight. That same order embedded teams of at least four people across federal agencies to review technology and spending systems.
A Pattern of Emergency Rulings Favoring DOGE
In June 2025, the court issued a 6-3 decision setting aside parts of a lower-court order and narrowing discovery about internal recommendations. CREW said the rest of the discovery order remained intact, and discovery was stayed while the D.C. Circuit modified it. On that same day, the justices also ruled 6-3 in Social Security Administration v. AFSCME to allow DOGE personnel access to restricted Social Security Administration databases, over dissents from liberal justices concerned about exposing private citizen records to unvetted personnel.
By December 2025, federal agencies including Defense, Agriculture and the EPA were citing embedded DOGE teams when executing budget cuts, contract cancellations and workforce downsizing across government, per USAFacts. CREW points to that reach as evidence DOGE exercised broad independent authority, even though DOGE's own temporary charter, established under Executive Order 14158 for an 18-month mandate, was scheduled to sunset on July 4, 2026.
Watchdogs Warn of a Broader Precedent
The watchdog group American Oversight has filed court briefs arguing that allowing DOGE to direct agency decisions while claiming advisory immunity under FOIA would set a precedent letting future administrations shield major government operations from public oversight simply by housing them inside the White House. The group's brief, filed with the Supreme Court, contends that functional power, not formal titles, should determine whether an office must comply with public records law.
The case arrives amid a string of related disputes over DOGE's footprint in government data and operations. With oral arguments now set for early 2027, the question of whether DOGE operated as a shielded advisory body or a FOIA-covered federal agency is headed for a final answer by next summer.

The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to hear the Trump administration’s case to prevent disclosure of records from the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).

Driving the news: A U.S. district judge previously ordered DOGE to comply with CREW’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, finding DOGE likely qualifies as a government agency subject to FOIA.
- The D.C. Circuit Court refused to halt the judge’s order; the Trump administration maintained DOGE is only an advisory body and exempt from FOIA under Supreme Court precedent.
- CREW seeks to investigate DOGE’s “secretive structure and operations,” particularly its involvement in mass workforce reductions and program cuts.
- Federal auditors have questioned DOGE’s claims of saving tens of billions of dollars, noting reporting errors and lack of supporting evidence.
- Auditors and Congress raised concerns about insufficient information on how DOGE handled sensitive data during its tenure.
Flashback: Elon Musk led DOGE for several months, ultimately leaving after a dispute with Trump over spending and tax policies; their relationship was later repaired.
- The Supreme Court earlier granted an emergency Trump administration request to narrow the scope of document requests, but further disclosure was upheld by lower courts, prompting the current appeal.
What we’re watching: The Court is expected to hear arguments and issue a ruling by the end of June.

(The Center Square) – The U.S. Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to take up a case determining whether a court is able to issue sweeping orders against executive advisory bodies, like the Department of Government Efficiency.
Justices on the high court agreed to hear U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, a case challenging a court’s ability to issue sweeping discovery orders against DOGE.
In February 2025, the D.C. District Court allowed a sweeping discovery order to move forward in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against DOGE, which argued that it did not fall under FOIA requirements because it served as an executive advising group, rather than an agency.
The dispute made it to the U.S. Supreme Court in June 2025, where justices ruled that the D.C. district court exceeded separation of powers authority in its decision. Since then, watchdog groups narrowed the FOIA lawsuit in an effort to obtain directives from DOGE administrators and gain access to data held by federal agencies.
The Trump administration urged the U.S. Supreme Court to rule against the watchdog’s lawsuit and define what kinds of orders a court may issue against entities like DOGE that advise the executive branch.
“Allowing the decision below to stand and far-reaching discovery to proceed would sow mischief in countless future cases against high-ranking officials,” Solicitor General John Sauer wrote in a petition to the high court. “Courts have already been grappling with a surge of improper attempts.”
The watchdog groups, however, argued that justices on the high court should determine whether it is appropriate for DOGE to be shielded from FOIA review. The group said FOIA regulations are meant to apply for all “establishments” within the executive office of the president.
“Under the government’s proposed test, a President wishing to evade FOIA could simply ‘informally delegat[e] authority’ to an entity within the [executive office of the president] by non-public memorandum, or draft intentionally ambiguous executive orders,” lawyers for the watchdog groups wrote.
Justices on the high court will likely hear arguments in the beginning of 2027. A decision in the case is expected by July 2027.
